newsitem.title: UK: Neuroleptic drugs may worsen dementia, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Neuroleptic drugs may worsen dementia, study finds.

text.p: Neuroleptic drugs, prescribed to calm the minds and behaviour of schizophrenics, seem to make some dementia sufferers even more aggressive and confused, British researchers said on Friday.

Psychiatrist Dr Rupert McShane and colleagues at Warneford Hospital in Oxford, who studied elderly patients suffering dementia, said any of several neuroleptic drugs may have made their condition worse.
They called for more tests to determine whether the drugs were appropriate for dementia sufferers.

"We are suggesting that people should regularly review the continuing need for using the medication and perhaps it would be a good idea to occasionally take patients off the medication and see whether they still need it," McShane said in a telephone interview.
Reporting in the British Medical Journal, McShane's group said they assessed 71 patients with dementia, mostly Alzheimer's, who were living at home.
They tested them for cognitive function such as whether they knew what day it was, behavioural problem such as aggression, sleep disturbances, hallucinations and delusions of persecution.
"The mean decline in cognitive score in the 16 patients who took neuroleptics was twice that in the patients who did not," they wrote.
It did not seem to matter how bad the dementia was -- all the patients who took the drugs got worse.
McShane said he did not want to cast doubt on how useful neuroleptics can be.

"They are used in schizophrenia and occasionally in severe mood disorders such as mania or depression. About a quarter of patients with dementia are likely to be prescribed them at some stage," he said.
"The evidence shows that in patients with schizophrenia, if anything their intellectual ability improves with neuroleptics because their hallucinations are better."
He said there could be a fundamental difference in the brain chemistry of patients with dementia that makes the drug act differently.
"The mainstay is good nursing care rather than drug treatment," he stressed.
